newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Platinum, palladium prices could rise more.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Platinum, palladium prices could rise more.

text.p: Platinum and palladium prices, which have risen about sharply in the past month, could rise even further if uncertainty about Russian supplies persists, analysts said Thursday.
Platinum prices have risen about 10 percent in the past month, while palladium prices gained 30 pct.
"Platinum and palladium prices are being driven by speculative buying, but there are good underlying fundamentals," Johnson Matthey, US metal sales manager said.

"News of the threatened strike at Norilsk, coming on top of the earlier breakdown in the Russia/Japan supply contract talks which cut supplies, has created a lot of uncertainty and if this persists prices could go higher still."
NYMEX April platinum was up $5.30 an ounce at $392.00 midday Thursday, after seeing a four month high at $399.80 on opening.
In the physical market platinum fixed at $393.50 in London Thursday, the highest level since Semptember 9, 1996.
NYMEX June palladium was up $3.65 an ounce at $153.90, after seeing a new contract high at $159.25 early.
Palladium fixed at $157.00 an ounce, the highest since July 11, 1995. The palladium sponge/plate differential was quoted $5.00-8.00 an ounce.
Workers at Russia's Norilsk mine have threatened to strike from March 15 over pay arrears, though management thinks a strike can be averted.

Earlier, in December 1996, the annual Russian/Japanese supply contract talks broke down, and no supplies of Russian palladium are likely in March, a spokesmsan for the Russian metal export agency, Almaz, said Monday.
But hedge funds have been capitalizing on the Russian supply difficulties, analysts said.
Earlier this month Julian Robertson of Tiger Management was reported saying his fund, with $8 billion under management, was building a palladium position.

"Demand has been good for platinum and palladium, but the users of palladium for electronics are now trying to replenish their inventories after allowing them to run down last year when they bought too much," Basset said.

"But (Russian President) Yelstin signed the 1997 budget yesterday which should open the way to the Russian's resuming supplies, though the palladium supply/demand balance is dependent on the Russian's being willing to sell more than they mine by running down their inventories," Basset said.
Russia is the world's second largest supplier of platinum, after South Africa, and the largest supplier of palladium.
Japan is the largest consumer of both platinum and palladium in the world.
Platinum is used in jewellery, electronics and in auto-catalysts for emission control, while palladium has similar uses.
In 1996 world supplies of platinum were estimated at 5.15 million ounces, of which Russian exports made up about 1.00 million ounces, according to New York industry consultants, CPM Group said.
"The platinum supply/demand balance has tightened sharply over the past three years, though probably remained in surplus last year, driven by Russian exports," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
World palladium supplies in 1996 were estimated at 6.79 million ounces, of which Russian exports comprised 3.5 million ounces, CPM Group said.

"Japanese palladium imports fell sharply in December 1996, suggesting the Japanese may not have been getting the supplies they needed even in late 1996 and this affected market psychology," US Platinum Institute spokesman, Dave Esrig said.

Japanese imports of palladium in December were 5,000 kilograms, down 30 pct from December 1995, while Japanese imports of palladium from Russia in December plunged to 2,700 kilograms from 4,100 in December 1995.
"But no-one believes the Russian palladium stockpiles are exhausted, it's just a temporary supply glitch," Esrig said.
